content.content:
# 02 Engine

The engine is everything below the screens: the typed mod project, the pipeline that turns it into artifacts, the test and delivery machinery, and the per-feature generators. All of it is **built** on the integration branch `feature/cyrus-r2` (see [11 history](11-history.md)), behind switches that default OFF ([reference/flags-and-env.md](reference/flags-and-env.md)). Each section ends with *Verified* (what actually ran) and *Not verified* (honest gaps); the per-feature long form with numbers is in [`docs/DOCUMENTATION.md`](../DOCUMENTATION.md) (heading list: [reference/documentation-index.md](reference/documentation-index.md)).

Contents: [ModSpec and revisions](#modspec-revisions-namespaces) / [router and adapters](#capability-router-and-adapters) / [version registry](#version-registry) / [build pipeline and service](#build-pipeline-and-the-build-service) / [Test Flight](#test-flight) / [delivery](#delivery-orchestrator-and-rollback) / [managed plugins, Pack Loader, pack hosting](#managed-plugins-pack-loader-pack-hosting) / [conflict engine and Mod Packs](#conflict-engine-and-mod-packs) / [import](#import-your-own-mod) / [data packs and worldgen](#data-packs-and-worldgen) / [creatures](#creatures) / [designers](#gameplay-designers) / [item states](#item-model-states-and-display-contexts) / [config studio core](#config-and-stats-core) / [motion core](#motion-core) / [meshgen and Blender](#ai-mesh-meshgen-and-blender) / [playtest, Doctor, telemetry](#playtest-bots-server-doctor-health-telemetry) / [Try It](#try-it-server) / [multi-version and legacy 1.21.1](#multi-version-builds-and-the-1211-legacy-path) / [networking and AI capabilities](#mod-capabilities-networking-and-ai) / [Mod lifecycle](#mod-lifecycle) / [eval](#eval-harness)

## ModSpec, revisions, namespaces
- **What.** `ModSpec` v1 (`lib/cyrus/engine-core/spec.ts`, Zod + committed JSON Schema `modspec.v1.schema.json`) is the game-agnostic content IR: items, mobs, abilities, GUIs, quests, recipes, loot, assets, datapacks, config, dependencies, acceptance tests. A project is an immutable chain of **revisions** (`revisions.ts`, `store.ts`); every revision traces to exact inputs and the engine release that built it; the last passing revision is always kept; revert = a new revision. Tables `CyrusProject`, `CyrusRevision` (a DB trigger keeps revisions immutable; smoke checks `cyrus_revision_immutable`), `CyrusProjectAsset`, `CyrusIdentifier`.
- **Namespaces and identifiers.** Each project reserves `nx_<hash>` at creation so ids, keys, permissions, sound keys, glyph codepoints and model paths are collision-free by construction (`identifiers.ts`; glyph block allocation for HUD fonts).
- **Plan gate.** `asset-gate.ts`: free/katara no assets, saka sound, all sound + texture; only create/edit is gated; fails closed.
- **Release record.** `release.ts`: engine release id (prompt version + sheets + rules + scanner hash + image digest), source/classpath/output hashes, scan report per build.
- **Compatibility.** Before r0 a "project" was a chain of `ModBuild` rows (`rootBuildId`/`baseBuildId`); both exist, the engine tables are additive (manual SQL `2026-10-10-cyrus-engine-core.sql`, **not applied** in production).
- Verified: unit + DB tests (`cyrus-engine-core`, `cyrus-engine-store-db`). Not verified: production data migration.

## Capability router and adapters
- **Router** (`engine-core/router.ts`, deterministic, no model): classifies what a request needs (plugin / plugin + resource pack / datapack / future client mod), discloses limits ("a vanilla client cannot show X"), applies the tier gate, and **downgrades instead of erroring**. The studio's separate broad-request router (`lib/cyrus/route.ts`, pure, zero API calls) routes prompts to games/categories/open mods.
- **Adapters** (`lib/cyrus/adapters`): the `GameAdapter` contract = artifact types and routes, toolchain + scanner, version list, knowledge source, **asset delivery per asset kind**, install rules, test lane, maturity (planned / template / beta / stable), route rules, optional `AssetProfile` (formats, channels, delivery, worker class, legal). Adapter #1 is Minecraft; `motion-minecraft.ts` lowers motion. Generated matrix: [reference/adapters.md](reference/adapters.md).
- **Per-game support packs** (`lib/cyrus/games/*.ts`, `GameSupport`): verified knowledge for Terraria, Valheim, Zomboid (and Palworld/Rust on WIP branches). These are knowledge + validators + compile harnesses only; those games are template previews in the UI and **on hold**.

## Version registry
`lib/cyrus/versions/registry.json` + `registry.ts`: the single source for JDK, pack formats (resource + data, major.minor), Paper API coordinate, **exact Paper server build and sha256 pin** (what Test Flight boots), capability flags (`legacyCustomModelData`, `dialogApi` ...), status (supported / preview / legacy / blocked) and `buildable`. Fail closed: a `null` pack number or missing server pin blocks the feature. Contract-tested against Paper's Fill API; a nightly check creates a "preview" row for new versions. Rendered table: [reference/versions.md](reference/versions.md). Facts: 1.21.1/1.21.4/1.21.8/1.21.11 build on JDK 21; 26.1.2 (build 74) and 26.2 (build 133) need JDK 25 and are **registered but not buildable** until the image has JDK 25 and an eval ran; 26.3 has only alpha/beta Paper builds, so it stays unpinned preview (an early research claim that 26.3 was stable was wrong and is corrected). `resourcePackClientVerified=false` everywhere: no real Minecraft client has loaded a Cyrus pack.

## Build pipeline and the build service
- **Service** `services/modbuilder` (Docker image on VM 88001; see [07 operations](07-operations.md)): `server.js` (HTTP), `prompts.js`, `route.js` (complexity routing, tiers), `precheck.js` + `rules/failure-rules.json` (18 reviewed rules), `sheets/` (per-version API sheets), `autofix.js` (deterministic fixes before a model repair), `scan.js` (bytecode + source safety scan), `jar.js` (reproducible jars: `jar --date`, sorted inputs), `release.js`, plus asset/designer/datapack/creature/config modules that bundle the `lib/cyrus` validators. Builds run Claude CLI with Read/Write/Edit only in a throwaway workspace, `javac --release N -proc:none` against a pre-resolved Paper-only classpath (Gradle only builds classpath files), no network for the model.
- **Models by tier**: Katara = Haiku class, Saka = Sonnet, Yakko = Opus (`MB_TIER_*`); complexity routing picks cheaper models for simple requests; repairs escalate one tier after two failed repairs. Knobs (all off by default): `MB_EFFORT`, `MB_CACHE_TTL`, `MB_DEDUPE`.
- **Portal side** `lib/modbuilder/create.ts` (`createModBuild`: validation, rate limits, 2-in-flight cap, token gate), `lib/cyrus/builder` (HTTP client), `lib/cyrus/follow.ts` (NDJSON re-attachable stream: stage -> `think`, `/live` draft -> `file`/`chunk`).
- **History**: service 0.3 (tuning) -> 0.4 (images the AI reads + live code) -> 0.5 (usage metering, auto-fixes, lean tools, cost knobs; branch only) -> 0.6 (networking capability manifest) -> r0+ (engine release record, asset/design/datapack/creature/config sections, catalog tools, designer no-model builds, legacy textures, JDK 25). Only 0.4 is running on VM 88001 per the last deploy; the rest requires the rebuild in the runbook.
- Verified: eval 28/28 built, 13/13 loaded on v6 (pre-programme); the programme added 178 eval prompts (harness built, **no paid run yet**). Not verified: AI output quality for texture/sound/datapack/import/designer/meshgen specs (no paid model build has run for them).

## Test Flight
`lib/cyrus/testflight` + `scripts` runner on node-2: a disposable Paper server per target version (pinned jar + sha256), boot, plugin enabled, RCON commands, `datapack list`, log matcher, clean shutdown; honest **per-check status table** (no "success" if a required stage was skipped); label "boot-tested" only where it ran. Measured: 26.x boots in about 10.4-10.8 s (722-803 MB RSS), 1.21.11 on JDK 21 in 18 s (878 MB); a whole flight 12-35 s. The **gate** (`CYRUS_TESTFLIGHT_GATE`, worker sweep) flies each succeeded build; `CYRUS_TESTFLIGHT_BLOCK_ON_FAIL` refuses installs of failed builds. One flight at a time (node-2 build lock); no container limits yet. Real flight records live in `/root/agent-notes/cyrus-research/*flights*.json` ([09 testing](09-testing-and-verification.md)).

## Delivery orchestrator and rollback
`lib/cyrus/delivery` + `lib/cyrus/assets` + worker: journaled install / update / uninstall of a jar, resource pack, data pack, worldgen pack or Mod Pack as one unit, through the existing Mods engine (`GameMod` source `cyrus` + `ServerMod` + worker `GAME_MOD_SYNC`; state file on the guest, backup, staged write, rollback). Honest states `rolled_back` and `rollback_incomplete`; Mod Packs re-check conflicts against the live server inside the orchestrator. Enqueue API `POST /api/cyrus/delivery/v1` (same checks as install, restart/worldgen acknowledgements, idempotency key, one job per server): contract in [CYRUS-DELIVERY-API.md](../CYRUS-DELIVERY-API.md). Flags `CYRUS_DELIVERY`, `CYRUS_DATAPACK_DELIVERY_REAL`, `CYRUS_MODPACK_INSTALL_REAL`, `CYRUS_MANAGED_PLUGINS_REAL`. Verified on real node-2 Paper: install, update, a deliberately broken update rolled back, uninstall, worldgen rollback, and (r38) a revoke mid-update that first failed to roll back (bug found and fixed) then restored exact bytes. Not verified: any customer server (by rule).

## Managed plugins, Pack Loader, pack hosting
- **Managed plugins** (`lib/cyrus/managed`, tables `CyrusManagedPlugin`, `CyrusServerManagedPlugin`): plugins Nxeon installs because Cyrus mods depend on them, pinned per Minecraft family, ref-counted, not removable while depended on. Hosts the **Nxeon Pack Loader** and **BetterModel 3.5.0** (MIT). Seed script `scripts/cyrus-seed-managed-plugins.ts`.
- **Pack Loader**: sends N packs by UUID with `addResourcePack`, per-pack required/optional, accept-rate telemetry, Geyser/Floodgate detection; `server.properties` only as a fallback (it holds just one pack). The conflict engine detects an existing pack owner (ResourcePackManager, Oraxen, Nexo).
- **Pack hosting** (`lib/cyrus/packhost`): content-addressed immutable URLs `/p/<sha1>.zip`, size caps (`CYRUS_PACK_MAX_BYTES`), retention GC, local or S3-compatible store (`CYRUS_PACK_STORE`); production with nothing configured has NO store (fail closed). The provider is not named to customers. Provider/domain choice is an open owner action.

## Conflict engine and Mod Packs
- **Inventory** (`lib/cyrus/inventory`): read-only scan of jars' descriptors (bytecode summary, plugin.yml, Fabric/Quilt/Forge/NeoForge descriptors), `server.properties`, datapacks, existing pack owners.
- **Static conflict engine** (`lib/cyrus/conflicts`, pure and deterministic: same input gives a byte-identical report): plugin names, commands/aliases (incl. Brigadier roots), permissions, depend/softdepend DAG, api-version/Java/Folia, events and priorities, NamespacedKey/PDC keys, legacy `custom_model_data` ints and `item_model` keys, recipe keys, sound keys, single-owner resources (Vault providers, chat, tab, sidebar), datapack `replace:true`, pack whole-file overrides, font codepoint overlap, budget classes. Severity: blocking / warn / info. Reserved namespaces prevent most clashes. A mutation corpus (take a good mod, collide IDs) tests catches.
- **Mod Packs** (`lib/cyrus/modpack`, API `/api/cyrus/modpacks/v1`, `CYRUS_MODPACKS`): an Nxeon manifest shaped like mrpack (files with path/sha1/sha512/downloads/env, override dirs, platform=paper); third-party jars by URL + hash, only Cyrus-built artifacts embedded; versioned; compatibility matrix; installs and rolls back as one unit; never contains Paper/vanilla jars. **Every open warning must be acknowledged** to install (owner recommendation applied, r29). Not plan-gated. r32 fix: pack create/install now enforce the same networking-consent and Test Flight gates as single installs. UI screens exist (r31).

## Import your own mod
`lib/cyrus/import` + `services/modbuilder/import.js`: source-only. Copies `src/main/{java,resources}`, ignores the uploader's build files (their build is never run), compiles with the service template and a **curated checksum-pinned dependency allowlist** (`import/deps.json`; first-class integrations Vault, LuckPerms, PlaceholderAPI). Unsupported: Kotlin, Lombok, annotation processors. Ingestion limits (zip-slip, zip-bomb ratio, nested jars, multi-release, class major), no execution at ingestion, ownership attestation record, detected licence, public sharing hard-off. Two scan profiles: strict for generated, **attested/imported** with warnings and no "safe" claim. Imported source becomes revision 0 and uses the same change planner, tests, versions and install path. Jar-only imports are analysis only. Not plan-gated (model use and assets follow tokens and gates). Flag `cyrus_import_enabled`. Fixed: import refused 1.21.9+ data packs (r31).

## Data packs and worldgen
`lib/cyrus/datapack`, `services/modbuilder/{datapack-spec,datapacks}.js`, `scripts/cyrus/datapack-derive.py`: a typed spec compiled by per-version emitters (the AI never hand-writes JSON); schema source vanilla-mcdoc (MIT); static validation (including a command allowlist and `line_continuation` refusal) then a real headless Paper over RCON. Content: recipes, loot tables, advancements, tags, functions, enchantments. **Worldgen** (R4: custom dimensions, biomes, structures; `CYRUS_WORLDGEN`): `/reload` does not reload worldgen, so these need a restart and a **broken worldgen pack stops a server at its next start**; hence delivery rollback is mandatory. Spans four datapack schemas and two `pack.mcmeta` styles (`min_format/max_format` from 1.21.9). Verified: worldgen showcase passed on 1.21.1/1.21.4/1.21.8/1.21.11/26.1.2/26.2; broken files each alone (validator 8/8, server refuses to start 7/8). Flags `CYRUS_DATAPACK_STUDIO`, `CYRUS_WORLDGEN`.

## Creatures
`lib/cyrus/creature` + `services/modbuilder/creatures.js` (`CYRUS_CREATURES`): `RigSpec` (3 archetypes, 5 procedural clips, 32 bones/creature, 4 creatures per server caps) compiled to a Blockbench `.bbmodel` for **BetterModel 3.5.0** (managed plugin, needs Java 25, so animated creatures are 26.x first; 1.21.x gets a vanilla-model mob with custom skin + full sound set, e.g. the banshee). Base vanilla mob supplies hitbox/AI; display entities carry the bones. Do not embed Blockbench (GPL). Verified on real Paper 26.2: load, pack hand-off + Pack Loader, malformed models, perf ramp 1/10/50; r30: creature paint is byte-identical inside BetterModel's pack. Not verified: how it looks or animates in a real client.

## Gameplay designers
All behind `CYRUS_DESIGNER` (+ `CYRUS_DESIGNER_BUILDS` for no-model builds). Design files live in `assets/designs/<id>.json` with a top-level `kind`; the compiler (`lib/cyrus/designer`, 39 files) emits a complete Paper plugin from a **verified Java component library**; every number/text becomes a `config.yml` setting, so edits change config only (proved with a config migration on real servers). Static + runtime **Budget** caps, no `run_command`, no arbitrary scripts. Javadoc/escape injection fixed in r32 (AC-3).
- **Item + ability graph (R3)**: 10 triggers, 11 conditions, 21 actions, 17-component library.
- **Menu + quest (R3)**: chest menus (click/drag cancel hardening, pagination, item/XP/Vault money prices, permissions, dialogues), quests (chains, 7 objective kinds, branches, daily/weekly, per-player progress in PDC).
- **Boss + encounter (R4)**: 20 vanilla bases, 1-5 one-way phases, up to 8 telegraphed attacks, arena (leash, enrage), boss bar, capped minions, drops by damage share, wave encounters; never persistent, no griefing.
- **HUD + glyphs (R4)**: action bar, per-player boss bars, per-player sidebar (never replaces another plugin's), plus the mod's own font `<ns>:hud` with codepoints from the identifier registry; 15 glyph presets; no shaders, no free positioning (the router says so).
- Verified by Test Flight RCON on 1.21.11 (JDK 21) and 26.2 (JDK 25): item, menu/quest, boss (55 RCON + 2 log checks), HUD (22 checks); scripted Mineflayer player 5/5 for the boss. Not verified: a real client seeing menus/HUD/bosses; other versions have no javac classpath for designers.
- **Designer edits reach servers (r31)**: no-model designer builds (config.yml-only = the base jar repacked with only config.yml changed; structural = javac) + delivery; real flight: edit -> build -> deliver -> RCON shows cooldown 100 and config migrated v1 -> v2. Image rebuild needed before enabling.

## Item model states and display contexts
`lib/cyrus/itemmodel` (`CYRUS_ITEM_STATES`): `ItemModelSpec` v1 with per-category defaults for **8 display contexts** (gui, ground, item frame, first/third person hands, head) and named STATES (bow pull stages, gun aim/reload) selected by 1.21.4+ item model definitions (`condition`, `range_dispatch`, `select`, plugin-set custom_model_data flags). No free animation (frame animation via `.mcmeta`, fast model switching). Vanilla-verified emitter and a real node-2 runner (javac 1.21.11 + 26.2, strict scan, Test Flight self-check, component round trip). The handgun grip default sits about 2/16 block off the hand in third person; the proposed fix is `CYRUS_HANDGUN_GRIP_FIX` (off, changes shipped packs, owner's call).

## Config and stats core
`lib/cyrus/config` (`CYRUS_CONFIG_STUDIO`): `ConfigSpec` v1 (12 param types, hard limits vs a "balanced" band, units, `applies` live/reload/restart, `visual` viewport links, presets), 12 category templates as data (mob, melee, gun, armor, ability, boss, shop, quest ...), the AI declares tunables and the build verifies they are read, **values-only revisions** delivered through the orchestrator (no model, no build), schema inference for imported mods. Real flights on 1.21.11 + 26.2; the "send to server" API returned 501 until the worker path landed (r31 closed it for designers). UI: [03 studios](03-studios.md).

## Motion core
`lib/cyrus/motion` (game-neutral, pure; plan: [motion/MOTION-PLAN.md](motion/MOTION-PLAN.md)): `MotionSpec` v1 with typed tracks (transform, particle, sound-cue, light/material, event/state-machine), deterministic `sample`, analytic seeded particles, a state-machine runner, simulation + event log, structured validation against a game capability's caps. 9 presets (gun fire, gun fire/reload/cock machine, hinged door, parametric humanoid/quadruped/floating gait generators, muzzle flash, explosion, fire, smoke, water splash). **Minecraft lowering** = designer kind `motion`: display-entity interpolation segments, step snaps, particle births, sound keys. Vehicles are explicitly NOT a Minecraft target (the core can express them; the build waits for a vehicle game). Real flights 39/39 RCON on 1.21.11 + 26.2; headless software-rasteriser sheets for review. Not verified: any look in a real client; studio timeline/preview build-out is future work.

## AI mesh (meshgen) and Blender
`lib/cyrus/meshgen` + `blender/` (`CYRUS_MESHGEN`, `CYRUS_MESHGEN_SCRATCH`; layer 4 of Model Studio): Zod specs for templates (rifle, crate, sword), a parts kit (10 shapes), a deterministic router over a **cost ladder** (rung 0 template ... rung 3 scratch script behind an AST guard), run headless in Blender 5.2.2 LTS inside a transient systemd sandbox (no network, user nobody, read-only fs, memory/CPU/task caps, build lock). Real node-2 flights accepted rifle/crate templates (1.4-2.5k triangles in about 26-29 s). Estimate-first job route + durable file queue + 30 s worker tick; the r32 driver-expression scan bypass (AC-2) is fixed. Not verified: a real model call, LODs, in-engine load, kernel escape (a microVM/gVisor is required before scratch scripts), an isolated GPU/worker; "drum magazine looks like a wheel"; parts overlap rather than union. Layer-3 meshes have **no export target** (no supported game takes glTF).

## Playtest bots, Server Doctor, health telemetry
- **Playtest** (`lib/cyrus/playtest`, `CYRUS_PLAYTEST`): a ModSpec's functional acceptance tests compile deterministically into a plan of 14 step kinds run by a Mineflayer bot inside Test Flight; verdict kept apart from the boot verdict. Ran on 1.21.11: a good fixture passed 6/6 and a deliberately broken one failed exactly the right checks. Other versions are refused, not skipped. Generated builds store no ModSpec yet, so playtest reports "not run" for them.
- **Server Doctor** (`lib/cyrus/doctor`, `CYRUS_SERVER_DOCTOR`, admin-only read-only API): server facts, plugin/mod inventory, conflicts, problems, warnings. Tested on a throwaway server seeded with a conflict, a throwing plugin, a legacy plugin and a Fabric mod; never run on a customer server.
- **Telemetry** (`lib/cyrus/telemetry`, `CYRUS_HEALTH_TELEMETRY`): opt-in, aggregate-only signals, retention; signed ingest answers 503 until the DRAFT tables exist; no collector exists. Open security items O-1 (replay) before enabling.

## Try It server
`lib/cyrus/tryit` (`CYRUS_TRY_IT`, `CYRUS_TRY_IT_EXPOSE`): a throwaway Paper server on node-2 with caps and auto teardown so a visitor can try a mod. Real flight: create -> pack served -> RCON -> a second session refused -> teardown. **Not public**: needs the firewall range 47200-47299 and DNS.

## Multi-version builds and the 1.21.1 legacy path
- `lib/cyrus/matrix` (`CYRUS_BUILD_MATRIX`): one design builds for several versions; real per-version compile + flight on 1.21.1/1.21.4/1.21.8/1.21.11 all passed; 26.2 refused as preview. Not wired into the builds route or stored yet.
- Legacy 1.21.1 item looks (`CYRUS_LEGACY_TEXTURES` portal, `MB_LEGACY_TEXTURES` service): custom model data on 52 vanilla-verified carriers, pack format 34, damage states only, every other limit shown; real Paper 1.21.1 flight 6/6. No real client.

## Mod capabilities: networking and AI
`lib/cyrus/capabilities.ts` + `services/modbuilder/capabilities.js` (default OFF, setting `cyrus_mod_networking_enabled`): a mod that wants the network ships an `nx-capabilities.yml` manifest (declared host allow-list, anti-SSRF via the NxHttp wrapper), the customer consents at install, and AI calls go through the Nxeon AI gateway (`lib/cyrus/ai-gateway*.ts`, a budgeted stub that never calls a model yet; gateway token expiry is open item O-2).

## Mod lifecycle
`lib/cyrus/lifecycle` + worker sweeps: install plans, on/off, broken/outdated detection (`cyrus-compat-watch`), updates, creator warnings. Game-version rules come from `GameSupport`.

## Eval harness
`lib/cyrus/eval`, `scripts/cyrus/eval-run.ts`, `services/modbuilder/eval/`: 178 prompts in categories with a per-version matrix and scoring spec; one-command runner with dry run, budget cap (required for a real run), resume, stage scoring, `baseline.json` + `report.md`. First run planned: 90 builds on 1.21.11 at Saka tier, estimated $9.73-$22.23. **No paid run has happened**; tested only against a fake CLI. See [09 testing](09-testing-and-verification.md).

content.thinking:
Since NxHttp isn't injected anywhere yet, I'll design the watchdog injection myself: after sanitizing the workspace but before validation/compilation, I'll place a fixed, audited NxPerf source file that gets overwritten each round so the model can't tamper with it, then require the plugin to call its init method via the prompt rules.

But relying on the model to actually call init is risky—if it skips that call, the watchdog does nothing. So instead I think the build service should deterministically rewrite the generated main class itself: locate the plugin.yml main class, find its onEnable method, and insert the NxPerf.init call as the first statement if missing, or synthesize an onEnable override entirely if none exists. This makes the injection automatic and independent of model cooperation.

Without that cooperation through budgets, the watchdog can still monitor TPS and MSPT using Paper's built-in APIs plus its own wall-clock tick measurements for responsiveness, but attributing lag to a specific plugin's features is hard without instrumentation—so the fallback is a generic "auto-disable heavy features" action that calls any registered disable callbacks, or does nothing useful if none are registered.

As a last resort, it could unregister all the plugin's own listeners and cancel its own scheduled tasks (not the server's), leaving only its watchdog task and commands active so status checks still work—effectively a safe mode. The risk is misattributing lag caused by other plugins and wrongly pausing itself, which is hard to avoid without real cost measurement since Paper removed built-in timings.

Writing timing wrapper code...

For scheduled tasks though, we can't easily wrap them for timing, so I need a fallback heuristic: attribute tick time as the sum of measured listener time plus cooperative timing sections, then flag a plugin if TPS drops below a threshold and its measured share exceeds roughly 25% of the tick budget.

I'm also thinking about budget enforcement — if a feature exceeds its per-tick budget, the work gets dropped or deferred rather than crashing, and we count these as overBudget events. The bigger gap is runnables like ChunkMirror's repeating task, which won't be measured at all unless we find a way to wrap scheduler tasks directly.

I'm weighing options: measuring our own tick-phase timing isn't precise, wrapping runTaskTimer calls feels too fragile, so maybe NxPerf should expose its own timer wrapper and the prompt rules require using it for repeating tasks, flagging raw runTaskTimer/BukkitRunnable usage as a precheck warning instead of a hard failure.

For attribution, I'm thinking of combining measured ms/tick from NxPerf-wrapped listeners and sections, plus a crude unmeasured-task detector counting the plugin's pending sync tasks, and triggering auto-disable when TPS drops below floor for a sustained window and either the measured share exceeds a default 10ms threshold or there are budget overrun events in that window.

Since I can't hook directly into CraftScheduler's internals, I'll rely on wrapping listeners to catch cases like a single blocking event handler, since even one huge-ms event should immediately trip the detector against the per-tick work budget.

For the fallback response itself, I'm figuring the plugin should unregister all our wrapped listeners and cancel our scheduled tasks (except the watchdog itself), call any cooperative pause callbacks so features can clear their queues, while still keeping commands functional. To support a resume command later, I need to retain the removed RegisteredListeners so they can be re-registered with HandlerList afterward.

Resuming is trickier for tasks: cancelled tasks can't just be un-cancelled, so true raw tasks probably need a restart to come back, but anything scheduled through our own NxPerf timer wrapper can be cleanly paused and resumed since we own the Runnable. For exposing a status command, I'm considering whether to hook into the plugin's existing command tree or register a brand new command dynamically through Bukkit's command map at runtime.

For `/<plugin> perf status`, I think the cleanest approach is wrapping the plugin's existing primary command executor so it intercepts "perf" as the first argument and falls through to the original executor otherwise, doing this registration a tick after onEnable once executors are set. If a plugin defines no commands at all, I'd need a fallback like registering a dedicated `/nxperf <plugin> status` command instead.

Permission-wise, perf subcommands should require op status or a `<plugin>.perf` permission node, checked via the sender directly.

For notifications, I'm thinking any online op gets a chat message on a trip event, alongside a structured warning log line with stable key=value fields like tps, mspt, and window size so it's machine-parseable.

For the periodic status heartbeat, I want `[NxPerf] status` lines logged every 5 minutes normally, but every 30 seconds during the first 15 minutes after enabling — giving a tighter watch window right after startup without being noisy long-term. I'm also sketching the config.yml schema: auto-disable toggle, tps-floor, window-seconds, max-work-per-tick, and max-ms-per-tick, all read from the plugin's config under a `perf.` namespace.

I'd rather avoid calling saveConfig at runtime since that strips user comments — instead, append the perf section textually into config.yml at build time if it's missing, and have NxPerf only read defaults at runtime without ever writing back to the file. That keeps the config deterministic and preserves any existing user formatting, though I need to check whether adding this section conflicts with Config Studio's schema validation.

For the budget API itself, I'm designing a cooperative rate-limiter where callers request work units each tick (like a mirror operation checking if it has budget before proceeding), and the budget resets lazily based on comparing the current tick to the last recorded tick using Paper's tick counter.

Now I'm sketching bounded work-queue helpers that process entries within a per-tick budget and drop overflow, plus a spawn limiter that caps entity creation per second and per chunk to prevent runaway spawning.

I want a reentrancy guard to stop my own code from recursing through its own events, implemented as a simple enter/exit depth counter wrapped in a guard helper, and I'm planning to separate the pure budget logic into a Bukkit-free class I can unit test with plain asserts on JDK21.

I need to split this into two files: `NxPerfCore.java` holding the pure logic (budgets, sliding-window TPS judge, rate limiter, decisions) with no Bukkit dependency, and `NxPerf.java` for the Bukkit glue, so the core can compile and run standalone test on node-2. I also want to verify `NxPerf.java` compiles against the classpath files for each of the buildable Minecraft versions.

#!/bin/bash
# Build one Test Flight fixture plugin jar the way the build service does (javac --release N -proc:none against the
# version's resolved classpath file, reproducible `jar --date`). Runs on the build host; fixtures are trusted code.
#   build.sh <fixture-dir> <api-version> <java-home> <release 21|25> <classpath.txt> <out.jar>
set -euo pipefail
SRC="${1:?fixture dir}"; API="${2:?api-version}"; JH="${3:?java home}"; REL="${4:?release}"; CP="${5:?classpath file}"; OUT="${6:?out jar}"
W="$(mktemp -d)"; trap 'rm -rf "$W"' EXIT
mkdir -p "$W/classes"
"$JH/bin/javac" -J-Xmx768m --release "$REL" -proc:none -encoding UTF-8 -cp "$(tr -d '\n' < "$CP")" -d "$W/classes" $(find "$SRC/src" -name '*.java' | sort)
sed "s/@API@/$API/" "$SRC/plugin.yml" > "$W/classes/plugin.yml"
( cd "$W/classes" && find . -type f | sed 's#^\./##' | sort > "$W/entries" )
args=(); while read -r e; do args+=(-C "$W/classes" "$e"); done < "$W/entries"
"$JH/bin/jar" --create --file "$OUT" --date 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z "${args[@]}"
sha256sum "$OUT"

I'm sketching out the stress spec shape, covering duration, baseline sampling, entity summon limits, chunk forceloading, and bot simulation options for placing/breaking blocks and walking around.

For the stress check itself, I'm defining a "stress" checkId with pass/fail/warn/not_run status plus raw sample data in the output. I'm deciding that stress should feed into requiredStages and affect the overall boot verdict only when a spec explicitly includes a stress config, mirroring how the playtest stage is treated separately from boot summarization.

Now I'm thinking through where the verdict-judging logic should live — I want a single authoritative function for computing the stress verdict from samples that both the runner and the TS gate can use without duplicating thresholds, considering whether TS can require a CommonJS lib from the services layer without violating the lib/cyrus import boundary.

For TPS sampling, I'm planning to query gametime at each sample and compute TPS as delta-gametime over delta-wall-seconds, accounting for RCON latency and tick-waiting noise at low TPS, plus parsing Paper's mspt average and counting entities via an execute selector.

For the load generator, I'm using a separate RCON connection to send summon and forceload commands concurrently so sampling doesn't get queued behind load traffic, since both still run on the main thread anyway. For chunk loading, I'll spiral forceload additions in 2x2 areas every 2 seconds within 200 blocks and remove them all at the end to simulate chunks loading over time.

I'm capping entities at ~2 pigs/second tagged for cleanup via kill command, keeping the total manageable since a naive mirrored-spawn approach across hundreds of loaded chunks would collapse TPS. For the bot workload, I'm simulating place/break actions 4 times per second near spawn plus periodic teleports to new chunks via RCON.

Default stress duration is 40s plus 5s baseline, adding roughly a minute of total runtime within the 420s timeout budget. I'm defining pass/fail thresholds: sustained TPS below 15 for 10+ seconds fails, below 18 warns, MSPT over 50 warns, RCON timeouts or server crashes fail, entity overflow fails as runaway entities, and a slow baseline marks the run as not_run since that indicates the test server itself was underpowered rather than the mod being tested.

For gate integration, the plan adds the stress flight when perf safety is enabled, with bot mode only used for compatible versions, and command lists derived from safe command labels. The harder question is honesty about coverage — the stress test can only verify events it actually exercises (spawns, chunk loads, block edits, commands), so if a mod's listeners hook into something unexercised like fishing events, there's no reliable way to detect that gap automatically.

I'm realizing the inventory module already does a bytecode scan of jars that extracts the plugin's listened event classes for the conflict engine, so I could reuse that summarizer during the gate to compare "events exercised by the stress test" against "events the plugin actually listens to," producing an honest coverage note listing what was and wasn't tested.

Still, timers run regardless of event coverage, so the pass verdict logic needs to account for the case where none of a plugin's listened events were triggered but its scheduled tasks ran fine under load -- I want to set verdict "pass" only when there's real overlap, rather than default-passing everything.

content.thinking:
I'm starting to write perf-risk.ts, defining types for severity levels and findings that capture the issue, reasoning, and safe-build constraints to append to prompts.

Now I'm sketching the detection rules themselves: deterministic regex patterns over normalized text that flag world-wide scope operations like "every chunk" or "all loaded chunks", while guarding against benign look-alikes like "the chunk you stand in" or "nearby chunks".

I'm also distinguishing severity levels — world-scope language alone is a warning, but combined with multiplicative actions (copy, mirror, replicate, duplicate across every block/event) escalates to critical, while per-player bounded actions like "every block you break" stay benign since they're inherently limited in scope.

For entities, "every entity in the world" per tick is high risk, but "every mob that spawns gets an effect" is a benign single-trigger event. Similarly, "infinite" or "unlimited" is usually benign when attached to specific items like durability, food, or flight, but becomes risky when paired with spawning or generation at scale.

I also want to flag recursive or chain-reaction patterns—mobs that split or spawn more mobs on death, explosions that trigger further explosions, TNT that creates more TNT—especially when there's no stated cap like "up to N" or "max N". And I should watch for per-tick loop phrasing as another marker of unbounded repeated work.

Beyond that, I'm setting thresholds for mass spawning (100+ mobs is high severity, 1000+ is critical, with words like "hordes" or "army of" as red flags) and for large radius/range values in blocks—64+ blocks is medium concern for per-tick scanning, higher values push toward high severity, though a one-time large-radius effect is less worrying than a repeated one.

I'm also flagging world-edit style operations that target the entire world or all chunks as critical, and noting that unbounded logs replayed on every chunk load represent a memory growth risk worth marking high. Config values like excessive chunks-per-tick settings or suspicious flags also warrant elevated concern, and explicit phrases like "crash the server" trigger an outright refusal.

For combination logic, I'm defining fan-out as replication-type verbs (copy, mirror, broadcast, etc.) paired with universal scope words (every/all chunks, players, blocks) combined with a per-event trigger — this multiplicative pattern of events times targets should be rated critical. Applying this to the ChunkMirror prompt, which copies every block change and mob spawn into every other chunk with a persistent replay log and aggressive config values, I'm concluding this deserves a critical rating with multiple contributing findings: the fan-out itself, the unbounded replay log, and mass entity spawning.

Now I'm designing safe alternatives for each finding — bounding the mirror radius to nearby chunks, capping the per-tick work queue, throttling mob mirroring to small per-chunk limits, and requiring opt-in start/stop commands — then appending these as explicit performance constraints to the original prompt before it reaches the build service. I'm also sketching out a set of roughly 40 golden test prompts, each paired with its expected severity level and rule IDs, including clearly benign examples to verify the system doesn't over-flag harmless requests.

I'll normalize the text and split it into sentences for proximity checks, then structure each rule as an object with an id, severity, test function, reason, and safe bounds, operating on the normalized text, sentence list, and extracted numbers.

Paper already exposes Server#getTPS() and getAverageTickTime() since around 1.16, so I can use those directly for status display instead of reimplementing TPS tracking myself. For measuring per-listener execution time, I'm planning to wrap each RegisteredListener for our plugin using HandlerList's static getRegisteredListeners(Plugin) call to find and intercept them.

For the pause/trip action, I'm weighing whether to unregister all of the plugin's listeners or keep protective ones active, since removing safety-related listeners could leave gaps in protection while paused.

A more targeted approach: only pause listeners whose measured cost is significant, say the top contributors making up roughly 90% of total cost, so cheap protective listeners stay active while expensive ones get disabled. For unmeasured scheduler tasks I can't attribute cost precisely, so I'm considering gating task-pausing behind a config option that defaults to true only when listener cost share is below some threshold.

For the second stage—canceling the plugin's own tasks—I don't have a clean way to measure their actual main-thread contribution, since tick-level events like ServerTickStart/End only give total tick duration, not per-plugin breakdown. So I'll gate this behind a perf.pause-tasks flag (default true), requiring TPS to stay below the floor for two consecutive windows and the plugin to have at least one repeating sync task, acknowledging the risk that another plugin could be the actual cause.

But if a server lags due to vanilla causes like huge farms, misattributing blame would stop timers across all Cyrus mods—too disruptive. So I'm defaulting stage 2 to off and documenting that only cooperative NxPerf.timer tasks get measured and paused automatically; the post-install watch catches genuine regressions by comparing TPS before and after install. content.thinking:
I'm designing a post-install watch module that monitors performance after enabling the safety feature, with a configurable watch duration and an automatic rollback or disable action if issues are detected.

For the detection logic, I'm planning out how to parse watchdog status lines, PAUSED markers, and lag warnings from logs, and how to judge whether a plugin is lagging, crash-looping, or already paused by an internal watchdog, with rules for when the outer watch should intervene versus defer to existing behavior.

For Paper's "Can't keep up!" lines specifically, I'm thinking through a baseline comparison: counting occurrences before and after an install, and only attributing lag to the mod if it's the sole change and the lag frequency and severity crossed set thresholds. I'm also considering whether TPS data should come passively from watchdog logs or be actively queried via RCON.

I'm designing a periodic sweep worker (cyrus-perf-watch.ts) that checks running servers every couple minutes for recently installed mods, pulls recent logs, and judges performance impact, emitting dedupe-tracked signals like PERF_LAG, PERF_DISABLED, or PERF_ROLLED_BACK, then takes action if the change is confirmed as real.

Realizing disabling a mod alone won't unload it since the plugin keeps running until restart, so I need a follow-up state where the next sweep detects the disabled mod with no active job and enqueues a one-time GAME_POWER restart, gated behind a configurable flag since restarting is disruptive but likely justified if the server is crawling at 1 TPS.

I want the crash-loop path to stay restart-free since the server's already restarting there, reserving the disable+restart action strictly for cases where the judge is confident the mod is the actual cause, never touching world data. For rollback, I'm considering only allowing it when a prior successful, stress-tested version exists, though that itself may need a restart via the update op — so I'll keep rollback as an optional, secondary action, and move on to designing the manual "disable this mod now" API control.

I need the API route to authenticate that the user owns the server, then enqueue a disable op with a restart flag so the worker handles it server-side even if the game server is laggy. I also need to locate where this should surface in the UI — likely the Mods tab on the server page where toggles already exist — and figure out how the worker's restart-after-disable logic should trigger the platform restart once the disable operation succeeds.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

I'm realizing that functions called from a tick function also run every tick via the call graph, but my rules only check the root function's runOn property, which seems acceptable per the doc. cd /tank/dev-worktrees/cyrus-perf && python3 - <<'EOF'
p='docs/cyrus/02-engine.md'
s=open(p).read()
s=s.replace(" / [Test Flight](#test-flight) / "," / [Test Flight](#test-flight) / [performance safety](#performance-safety) / ",1)
old="## Delivery orchestrator and rollback"
new='''## Performance safety
Born from the 2026-10-11 ChunkMirror incident (a mod built exactly as asked: every block change and mob spawn copied into every chunk, chunks-per-tick 500; it passed compile, scan and the boot-only Test Flight and took the owner's 2-core server to 1 TPS). Master switch `CYRUS_PERF_SAFETY` (default **ON**; `0` = kill switch), build service `MB_PERF_SAFETY` (default ON). Five layers:
1. **Perf-risk classifier** (`lib/cyrus/safety/perf-risk.ts`, pure, deterministic, client-safe): rules for fan-out mirroring, replay logs, per-tick world scans, world-wide iteration, recursive spawns, cascading explosions, mass spawns, unbounded growth, spreading blocks, huge radius, lag intent, and config values (per-tick, radius, mob copying). Each finding has a plain reason and a SAFE bounded alternative; `mustConfirm` at high/critical. Planner contract: show it before any hold, default = build the safe version (`applyPerfChoice` appends a PERFORMANCE LIMITS block), "Build anyway" = `as_asked`; `perfPreBuildCheck` is the server twin (409 `perf_confirm`). Golden set: 41 prompts incl. ChunkMirror and benign look-alikes. Wiring into the plan screen belongs to the planner branch (fix/cyrus-live-test-1).
2. **NxPerf watchdog** (`services/modbuilder/perf/`, injected by `perf.js` into `<main package>.nxperf` before every javac of a generated plugin; imported plugins untouched): real TPS each second, main-thread time of the plugin's own listeners (wrapped once after onEnable), pause of the plugin's costliest listeners + NxPerf timers/queues (never the server, never another plugin) when TPS < `perf.tps-floor` (15) for `perf.window-seconds` (10) while the plugin uses >= 25% of each tick, or it alone exceeds `perf.max-ms-per-tick` (25) for the window, or one tick of its listeners takes > 2 s; logs `[NxPerf] PAUSED ...`, tells online operators; `/<command> perf status|pause|resume`; status lines every 30 s for 15 min, then every 5 min. Cooperative API the prompt REQUIRES (rule 10 + API sheet): `take`, `queue`, `timer`, `spawnAllowed`, `rate`, `enter/exit`, `radius`. PERF pre-check (`perfcheck`, `configCheck`): world iteration, spawns/explosions/block changes/chunk loads in loops, raw repeating tasks, events fired inside handlers, `while(true)`, huge radius literals, config per-tick > 256 / radius > 64 / mob copying on; hits go back to the model once and stay as scan notes. Failure rule `perf-unbounded-fanout`. Limits it cannot see: work inside raw scheduler tasks the model wrote anyway (not measured), async threads (not allowed anyway).
3. **Test Flight stress phase** (runner `tf-lite-5`, `stress-lib.js`, `stress-bot.js`, `lib/cyrus/testflight/stress.ts`): after the boot checks, baseline samples, then 40 s of load (passive mobs summoned over RCON, chunks force-loaded on a spiral, the mod's bare commands once, and on bot-verified versions (1.21.11) a Mineflayer player placing/breaking blocks and teleporting) while sampling the real tick rate (delta `time query gametime` / wall clock), MSPT, entities, RSS. Verdict pass / warn / fail with numbers (fail: TPS < 15 for >= 10 s, a 10 s stall, > 2500 entities, a crash; warn: TPS < 18 sustained, MSPT > 50, RSS +400 MB; `CYRUS_STRESS_*` settings); honest `not_run` when the host itself was slow or the load fired none of the mod's events (coverage from the jar's own event handlers, watchdog excluded). Stored as `StoredFlight.stress`; a FAILED stress **blocks Install by default** (`flightBlocks`, independent of `CYRUS_TESTFLIGHT_BLOCK_ON_FAIL`; `CYRUS_PERF_BLOCK_ON_FAIL=0` turns it off) with the measured numbers. Switch `CYRUS_TESTFLIGHT_STRESS` (default on with perf safety; flies only where the gate flies).
4. **Post-install watch** (`lib/cyrus/safety/perf-watch.ts` pure judge + `worker/cyrus-perf-watch.ts`, sweep `cyrus-perf-watch` every 2 min, `CYRUS_PERF_WATCH` default on): for 15 min (`CYRUS_PERF_WATCH_MINUTES`) after a Cyrus install/update it reads the game log (read-only) and acts once when the new mod is the cause: its own watchdog readings under the floor with a high share, Paper "Can't keep up" warnings when it was the only change and the server did not lag before, or a crash loop pinned on it. Action `CYRUS_PERF_WATCH_ACTION` = disable (default: engine disable, config kept, then restart, `CYRUS_PERF_WATCH_RESTART`) / rollback (previous version whose stress did not fail) / notify; owner told in-app + email. Acts only with `ENABLE_REAL_GAMEMODS=1`; never deletes data. **Disable this mod now** on the server's Mods tab (`disableCyrusModNow`): switch off + restart through the worker, works while the server lags.
5. **Emitters audit** (`lib/cyrus/safety/perf-caps.ts`, test-pinned): designers, motion, data packs and worldgen already had per-activation / plugin-wide caps; added for data pack tick functions: unconditional summon refused, particles <= 64 per command (1000 anywhere), fill/clone <= 64 blocks, unfiltered `execute as @e` warned. Owner decision: a cooldown-0 designer click ability has no per-player floor (adding one changes every existing designer jar).
- Verified: unit tests (perf-risk, watchdog injection, stress, watch, caps); real node-2: watchdog + a demo plugin compiled and strict-scanned clean on 1.21.1/1.21.4/1.21.8/1.21.11, NxPerfCore JVM test 19/19; ChunkMirror stress flights (records `/root/agent-notes/cyrus-research/perf-flights-2026-10-11.json`). Not verified: a real model build with the new prompt (no paid run), any customer server (by rule), the post-install watch against a live log, a real client.

## Delivery orchestrator and rollback'''
assert old in s; s=s.replace(old,new,1)
s=s.replace("label \"boot-tested\" only where it ran.","label \"boot-tested\" only where it ran. Since perf safety a **stress phase** follows the boot checks ([performance safety](#performance-safety)).",1)
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF
grep -n "## Performance safety" docs/cyrus/02-engine.md

content.thinking:
The watchdog never tripped because node-2's TPS stayed high (median 19.77) and MSPT only peaked at 57 — the thresholds for TPS and budget verdicts weren't crossed. So the real culprit wasn't CPU slowdown but runaway entity count, which the watchdog's current checks don't account for.

I'm sketching a non-cooperative "entity runaway" guard: track spawns via CreatureSpawnEvent while flagging when our plugin's own listener/timer code is executing, so we can attribute spawn bursts specifically to our plugin's activity and trip a pause if spawns exceed a per-second or per-tick threshold. I'm designing a SpawnGuard listener with a depth counter around our callEvent/Timer logic to mark "inOwn" execution windows, careful to exclude our own internal listener from being paused by its own wrapper.

Rather than just counting, I decide it's better to actively cancel excess entity spawns above a configurable cap (e.g. 50/second) and only trigger a full pause if denials persist for several seconds — effectively a hard spawn-rate limiter for runaway plugins. I also note the SpawnGuard listener itself needs to be excluded from the generic listener-wrapping logic, and that spawns from raw scheduler tasks outside our tracked "own" context won't be counted, only those happening inside event handlers we're monitoring.

Now I need to add this spawn cap to the config with proper clamping, surface it on the status line, and recompile before rerunning the unbounded-with-watchdog stress flight to confirm entity counts stay controlled.

entries.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.
